title: Typert Gateway Targeted Method Calls
summary: A business service marks methods as remotely callable with a decorator; the Typert generator produces a typed client projection from them, and the API gateway carries each call as one request and one result.
firstReason: The browser no longer calls typed methods from generated TypeScript: the Go host handles form and htmx requests directly, and remote callers such as the SDKs use the JSON-RPC protocol, so decorators and generated projections are not needed.

title: Session history, control state, and Remote event transport
summary: Browser data comes in three kinds with different recovery rules: the session log is paged and followed by sequence cursor, control state is sent as complete snapshots, and notifications are fire-and-forget. The API gateway owns the stream transport; controllers own their own wire types.
firstReason: The three recovery rules are kept, but the carrier changes from WebSocket remote streams consumed by a client runtime to server-sent events that carry rendered fragments and resume by sequence number.

title: Workspace file service
summary: A dedicated host service reads workspace files for the UI with bounded line pages, byte windows and capped whole-file reads, names files by absolute path in the session's execution world, and reports changes; the session controller holds no file code.
firstReason: The Go UI needs the same bounded file reads through the session's filesystem backend; only the client-side provider half becomes server rendering.

title: Workspace file read authority
summary: Reading or inspecting a named file follows the session filesystem backend's read authority, so a path outside the workspace is readable when the backend allows it; listing and change watching stay limited to the workspace.
firstReason: One read policy, owned by the filesystem backend, avoids a second inconsistent check in the UI layer; keep it, together with the stated exposure of HTML preview.

title: User-terminal permissions
summary: The sidebar terminal a person types into runs with the operating-system user's own permissions, not inside the agent's sandbox, and asks for no agent approval. Changing the agent's sandbox mode leaves user terminals running, and their input and output are not model input.
firstReason: The separation between what the person may do and what the agent may do is a product rule. Without it a person must widen the agent's sandbox to do manual work. The subprocess provider's scrubbing of credential environment variables still applies.

title: Writer acquisition for blank Session reuse
summary: Opening a workspace reuses an existing blank session only after the host has acquired that session's writer lock; if another host holds the lock it creates a new session. The agent keeps the lock for its lifetime, and no process id is persisted.
firstReason: Two hosts sharing one storage directory can otherwise pick the same blank session. Acquire-then-use closes the race that check-then-release leaves open, and it does not depend on the runtime.

title: Binary workspace file transfer
summary: File previews receive raw bytes instead of base64 text: one `readBytes` Remote method with an optional byte range, with the generated RPC codec carrying byte buffers as multipart attachments.
firstReason: The goal (no base64 overhead, ranged reads, one authorization path) stands. With a server-rendered UI the browser fetches file bytes over ordinary HTTP with a Range header from the Go host, which already shares routing, session lookup and error handling; the Typert byte codec is not needed.

title: Remote duplex stream: one kind of stream, an uplink channel, and an invocation context
summary: Every Remote stream is bidirectional over one multiplexed WebSocket: the method's return type declares the downlink and uplink item types, and the host method reads the uplink and the caller identity from an invocation context. Reconnect and resume are left to higher layers.
firstReason: The Go UI receives live updates over server-sent events and sends input as ordinary HTTP requests, so a generated duplex RPC stream is not its transport. What carries: one kind of stream, an explicit per-invocation context (caller identity, cancellation signal), and resume owned by the layer above. The terminal island and the SDK may still need a duplex channel, which the API area must decide.

title: Open the Session when migration is required
summary: Background actions (fork from the session list, listing projections) do not trigger a session format migration. They check the stored format first and, if migration is needed, refuse and offer to open the session, which is the only action that migrates.
firstReason: A migration is slow and writes a new generation, so it should follow an explicit open. The Go format starts at one version (DH-ADR-2), but the rule should be in place before its first migration exists.

title: Peer-scoped connect handshake
summary: Automation callers (CLI, MCP) obtain their own peer through a connect endpoint and must opt in to receive human interactions; the default is none. Browsers keep sharing one owner peer that may answer.
firstReason: A method-only caller that is subscribed automatically can receive and answer an approval meant for a person. Opt-in participation and per-peer cleanup are security rules; the cookie versions and the redirect are wire detail that need not be kept (DH-ADR-2).

title: Peer principals and method-level Remote access control
summary: Every caller connection (peer) carries a principal, the identity that permission decisions read. Each Remote method declares the resource it acts on, and the gateway asks a role-based access service before dispatch. There is no implicit operator fallback.
firstReason: Without it a host method cannot tell whom a call speaks for, or restrict it. Principal, peer, per-method resources and one decision point are the authorization model for the Go API. Inference: Go handlers declare their resource at registration instead of through a TypeScript decorator.

title: Compress the Remote stream WebSocket with permessage-deflate
summary: The multiplexed stream WebSocket is compressed with permessage-deflate at level 1 by default, and frames under 1,024 characters are sent uncompressed.
firstReason: The goal (less traffic over tunnels and slow links without adding latency to small token frames) stands. The Go UI streams over server-sent events, so compression is HTTP response compression with a flush after each event; the tuning is redone for that transport.

title: Session snapshots, passive subscriptions, and Web aggregation
summary: Session access is split into six independent operations: a snapshot and an observation each for history, projections and state. Follow and wait are compositions of these, and subscribing does not force a read.
firstReason: Mixing point reads, subscriptions and the web conversation opening made passive observers do unnecessary reads and left a gap between read and subscribe. The Go API and the server-rendered conversation view both build on the same six operations.

title: whenAccess registration that follows access
summary: A client plugin can register sidebar entries, panels and streams 'while access holds': the registration is installed when the current caller gains a permission and removed when it loses it.
firstReason: The Go host decides what to render per request from the caller's permissions, so entries a caller may not use are not in the page. What must be designed instead is re-rendering when a permission changes during a session.

title: Image reads use attachment-store access
summary: Reading an image needs permission on the attachment store plus a complete content-addressed reference. The host no longer scans the session's history to prove that the session mentions the image.
firstReason: The scan cost grew with history length and located nothing, because the path follows from the content hash. Inference: the Go design keeps this, but must state plainly that any authorised caller holding a reference can read any image in the store.

title: Present single-Session migration through follow redirection
summary: Proposed, not built: when opening an old session needs a format migration, the history read returns a typed 'migration' reference; the client follows its progress and failure, then returns to the history read. Progress never enters the session log.
firstReason: Adopt, at low priority. The Go format has no migrations at first (DH-ADR-2), but the first one will need visible progress and failure that stay out of the event log. The proposal leaves open whether 'done' means prepared in memory or published, and the Go spec must choose.

title: Session retain facets and recently viewed Sessions
summary: A client Session reference states what it keeps alive: the event connection, and named facets of derived computation. Recently viewed sessions stay retained so returning to one does not pull history again, while expensive derived work runs only for references that ask for it.
firstReason: The goal (switching back to a recent session is instant, and idle sessions do not pay for derived work) stands. The Go UI keeps session state on the host, so the equivalent is a host-side cache of rendered conversation state with an eviction rule, not browser object retention.

title: Keep accepted Session presentation across list refreshes
summary: The client's session manager remembers which sessions have had a prompt accepted, so a later list refresh or reconnect that still reports the session as blank does not turn its row back into New Session.
firstReason: The symptom comes from a browser-side mirror racing the host's list. With a server-rendered list the host is the only source, so the Go design must instead mark a session as no longer blank at prompt acceptance, before the turn starts.

title: Session opening cache identity and read ordering
summary: The prepared-observation cache identifies its producer by a per-instance identity token plus the log revision, so access through a proxy no longer invalidates it falsely. Auxiliary client requests (skills, commands, goals, references) wait until the conversation's initial open succeeds before they touch a cold log.
firstReason: The goal (opening an old session causes one cold read, not several competing ones) stands. Go can compare the service instance directly and collapse concurrent opens into one in-flight read, and under DH-ADR-3 the host orders the auxiliary reads itself.

title: A reused blank Session runs the requested preset
summary: `session.create` treats a named session id as a reuse candidate that the host verifies (no turn started, right directory, unarchived member of the workspace, no other writer). A reused blank session runs the requested preset, not the one its log recorded; a candidate that fails a check is left unchanged and a new session is created.
firstReason: It stops a removed or renamed preset from breaking every new conversation in a workspace. Host-side verification under the write lease is language-neutral.

title: Time-sliced Session-list work
summary: Session-list assembly works against a monotonic deadline (`listWorkSliceMs`, default 16 ms) and yields to the event loop only when a slice is used up, so a large list does not monopolize the host and a small one pays no extra round trips. Cancellation is checked per row and no partial list is returned.
firstReason: Cooperative yielding exists because Node runs host work on one thread. In Go the list is built on its own goroutine and the scheduler preempts it; the parts to keep are cancellation through the request context and never returning a partial list.

title: Web sidebar terminals
summary: A person can open interactive shells in the sidebar. The host owns each terminal by session and stays authoritative for process, title and screen contents; the browser renders with xterm.js, attaches with a bounded screen snapshot followed by ordered output, and a browser disconnect or tab switch leaves the process running.
firstReason: Host-owned processes with views that can reattach fit the Go design, and the terminal is one of the JavaScript islands DH-ADR-3 names. Create that is idempotent on a caller-chosen id, and cleanup in the background, are worth keeping as written.

title: Two-hour reclamation of unattended browser terminals
summary: A browser terminal is reclaimed only after no window has held it and the host has confirmed it idle for two continuous hours. Running or unknown activity cancels the deadline, and a returning window reattaches the same process.
firstReason: Abandoned shells otherwise live forever, and killing on disconnect would lose running work. The policy is host-side and language-neutral.

title: On-demand watching and automatic refresh for Sidebar previews and file trees
summary: Sidebar previews and file trees refresh from on-demand operating-system file watches. A preview watches its file and the files it references; the tree watches only the direct entries of open directories and releases a watch on collapse. Watches carry invalidation only, and content is read again through the normal readers.
firstReason: Changes come from shells and editors as well as harness tools, so only operating-system watching is complete, and watching only what is open bounds the cost. The Go host needs a file-watching library in place of chokidar and pushes invalidations over its event stream.

title: Manual generation continuation
summary: After an eligible model failure, a play action submits an empty prompt whose source is `retry`. The ordinary admission path records an empty user message and opens a new balanced turn, and the failed turn stays closed. A fixed allowlist of six failure codes decides eligibility.
firstReason: Reusing ordinary message admission avoids a special loop branch and a new durable event, and no artificial instruction enters the history.

title: Chat history consumption classes and interactions
summary: Proposal: the class-level design behind history prefetch, saying which client object owns the network request, which owns the decision to show the page, and how they call each other.
firstReason: The Go design should not carry this over: it describes interactions between client-side session and chat classes that do not exist when the Go host renders the HTML (DH-ADR-3). The behaviour it implements is kept through the companion note on history prefetch.
